overview.text: Colin Luther Powell (1937–2021) was a U.S. Army officer and diplomat who rose from ROTC at New York’s City College to become a senior national-security official. He served two tours in Vietnam, became chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in 1989, and oversaw U.S. military operations including the 1991 Gulf War. Appointed by President George W. Bush, Powell served as secretary of state from 2001 to 2005—the first African American to hold that office. His legacy also includes his February 2003 presentation to the UN Security Council arguing that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction; later reviews found some of the intelligence behind the presentation was erroneous.

key_facts.text: Powell was born in Harlem to Jamaican immigrant parents and grew up in the South Bronx.
After joining ROTC at City College of New York, he was commissioned as an Army second lieutenant in 1958 and served two tours in Vietnam.
He became chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in 1989; during his tenure, he oversaw the 1991 Gulf War operation, Desert Storm.
Powell served as secretary of state from 2001 to 2005 and was the first African American to hold the position.

In his February 5, 2003, UN Security Council address, Powell presented U.S. intelligence supporting claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. Later official reviews found some of the intelligence was erroneous and that serious doubts about a key source had not reached Powell before the speech.
